England.difference_en: England Year 1 begins by recognising and naming common 2D shapes, then classifies them increasingly by sides, angles and parallel relationships. China's primary progression also develops recognition and classification through geometric properties.
England.why_en: A shape concept should depend on invariant properties rather than a fixed orientation or typical appearance.
England.classroom_use_en: Show the same shape in different sizes, colours and orientations and ask why it remains in the same class.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 1-3 emphasise recognising, drawing and classifying shapes by defining attributes.
US.why_en: This separates properties that define a shape from non-defining features such as colour, size or orientation.
US.classroom_use_en: Ask which property could change without changing the shape's class, and which property could not.

England.difference_en: England Years 1-2 identify common 3D shapes and their faces, edges and vertices; Year 5 also reasons from 2D representations of 3D shapes. Revised PEP introduces solid shapes in Grade 1 upper and later returns to composite solids and prisms.
England.why_en: Handling physical objects reduces errors caused by judging hidden faces from a flat drawing only.
England.classroom_use_en: Count faces, edges and vertices on a solid first, then identify which parts are hidden in a 2D drawing.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 1-2 compose and analyse 2D and 3D shapes and their attributes.
US.why_en: Composing and decomposing shapes develops part-whole structure and spatial visualisation.
US.classroom_use_en: Build different solids from the same number of unit cubes and compare their structures.

England.difference_en: England Years 4-6 increasingly classify triangles, quadrilaterals and other polygons by properties.
England.why_en: Classification should preserve hierarchy: for example, a square also satisfies the definition of a rectangle.
England.classroom_use_en: Use always/sometimes/never questions to test hierarchical shape relationships.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 3-5 explicitly build shape categories and subcategories from shared attributes.
US.why_en: Hierarchical classification turns definitions into logical inclusion relationships rather than mutually exclusive labels.
US.classroom_use_en: Draw a classification diagram showing square → rectangle → parallelogram relationships.

England.difference_en: England Year 3 explicitly uses horizontal, vertical, parallel and perpendicular relationships and later applies them in shape classification. Revised PEP develops line and angle relationships and later parallel/perpendicular properties in quadrilaterals.
England.why_en: Parallel and perpendicular describe relationships between lines and do not depend on page orientation.
England.classroom_use_en: Include slanted parallel and perpendicular examples rather than only horizontal and vertical ones.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 explicitly identifies and draws parallel and perpendicular lines and uses them in shape classification.
US.why_en: Connecting line relationships with shape properties supports classification and angle reasoning.
US.classroom_use_en: Identify all parallel and perpendicular relationships in a quadrilateral before classifying it.

England.difference_en: England recognises polygons and quadrilaterals from Year 3 and refines classification by angles, sides and parallel relationships through Years 4-6.
England.why_en: Precise properties make shape names useful tools for reasoning rather than visual labels.
England.classroom_use_en: Classify a set of non-prototypical quadrilaterals using definitions rather than appearance.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 explicitly develops shared quadrilateral attributes and Grade 5 builds a hierarchy of 2D shape categories.
US.why_en: This supports inclusion relationships such as a square also being a rectangle.
US.classroom_use_en: For one shape, list every category it belongs to and justify each classification.

England.difference_en: England Year 6 identifies radius, diameter and circumference and knows that the diameter is twice the radius; primary mathematics does not formally require the circle-area formula. China's third learning stage goes further into circumference and area, with revised PEP Grade 6 upper containing a Circle unit.
England.why_en: This is a genuine difference in curriculum depth and should not be reduced to same-grade matching.
England.classroom_use_en: Separate circle parts and relationships from circumference/area calculation when comparing the curricula.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 1-6 recognise circles as shapes but do not develop radius, circumference and area as a formal primary measurement strand; more systematic circle work occurs later.
US.why_en: There is no direct Common Core Grades 1-6 equivalent to China's primary circle-area content.
US.classroom_use_en: Show that the baseline has no equivalent primary requirement rather than forcing a Grade 5 or 6 match.

England.difference_en: England uses whole, half and quarter turns from Year 1 and formally connects angles with turn in Year 3. China's geometry progression also develops angle meaning and measurement through primary school.
England.why_en: Movement and turning experiences keep angle from being understood only as a static picture of two lines.
England.classroom_use_en: Use body turns, pointers and opening doors to establish the idea of how much turn has occurred.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 formally defines angles from two rays sharing an endpoint and measures them in degrees; earlier direction activities do not form the same explicit angle-as-turn progression.
US.why_en: Formal angle study is more concentrated in Grade 4.
US.classroom_use_en: Before using a protractor, use quarter-turn and half-turn benchmarks for 90° and 180°.

England.difference_en: England Years 3-5 develop right-angle benchmarks, acute/obtuse classification, then estimation and measurement in degrees.
England.why_en: Angle size depends on the amount of turn or opening, not on how long the arms are drawn.
England.classroom_use_en: Compare angles with different arm lengths but the same opening before measuring them.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 defines one degree as 1/360 of a circle and treats angle measure as a count of unit angles.
US.why_en: Degrees therefore have a measurement-unit meaning rather than being arbitrary numbers on a protractor.
US.classroom_use_en: Estimate whether an angle is nearer 90° or 180° before measuring.

England.difference_en: England Years 3-4 formally identify right, acute and obtuse angles, with later extension to reflex angles.
England.why_en: Angle type is determined by size range, not by orientation.
England.classroom_use_en: Rotate the same acute angle into several orientations and keep the classification unchanged.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 works with angle measure and perpendicular relationships but does not organise all angle-type names as the same standalone progression used in England.
US.why_en: The curriculum structures differ while sharing core angle measurement and relationship work.
US.classroom_use_en: Compare the specific standard requirements rather than using the number of angle-category names as a depth measure.

England.difference_en: England Year 5 explicitly measures angles in degrees with a protractor and draws angles of specified size.
England.why_en: Correct protractor use depends on the vertex, baseline and direction of the scale.
England.classroom_use_en: Estimate the angle first, then check whether the inner or outer protractor scale is appropriate.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 already requires measuring and drawing angles with a protractor.
US.why_en: Formal angle measurement appears about one school year earlier in the Common Core baseline than in England's statutory progression.
US.classroom_use_en: Treat the timing as a progression difference, not a quality judgement.

England.difference_en: England Years 5-6 use angles on straight lines, full turns, triangles and polygons to find unknown angles.
England.why_en: Unknown-angle problems shift work from direct measurement to reasoning from known relationships.
England.classroom_use_en: When an angle can be deduced, ask pupils to write the relationship before allowing a protractor.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 explicitly treats angle measure as additive and uses addition/subtraction equations to find unknown angles; more systematic polygon-angle work comes later.
US.why_en: Grade 4 first establishes that larger angles can be decomposed into smaller angle measures and recombined.
US.classroom_use_en: Split one larger angle into two parts and represent the total with an equation.
